1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop to work along the long diagonal and keeps the centre squares under watch from a distance. White holds back the d-pawn and stays flexible, accepting that Black may stake out the centre at once; the game becomes strategic rather than tactical.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece to a square that watches d5 and e4 and keeps every pawn set-up open for later. The cost is that White lets Black choose the structure: a solid blocked centre, a symmetrical pawn formation or an attack on the knight are all available.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.b3.strategy: Prepares the queenside fianchetto, so the bishop will look down the long diagonal. But it does nothing for the centre or for d5, and Black can take the central squares at once and hit c4. Sound enough, yet Black reaches easy equality.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.b3 d5.strategy: Plants a pawn in the centre and attacks the c4 pawn at once, before White's bishop on b2 can bear on the long diagonal. Black gets a solid pawn pair and free development, so White has spent a move on the fianchetto without gaining central space.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and puts the c4 pawn to the question. White's fianchettoed bishop will lean on the d5 pawn and the queenside, so Black gets a solid pawn pair in return for a long game of pressure that White steers.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6.strategy: Answers the fianchetto with one of its own: the bishop on the long diagonal will contest the squares White's bishop wants, above all e4. Black leaves the centre to White for now and relies on controlling it from a distance, which asks for accurate timing later.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Romanishin Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that prepares to hit the c4 pawn with the b-pawn. It develops nothing and does not contest the centre, so White has a free hand to finish development; the point is that the queenside advance can be played with tempo once the position allows.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Bg2.strategy: The natural development: the bishop takes the long diagonal, aimed at b7 and the a8 corner once the f3 knight steps aside, which makes the planned queenside advance awkward for Black. White simply finishes development and lets the slow move show.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Bg2 b5.name: English Opening: Romanishin Gambit
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 a6 4.Bg2 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn: after cxb5 axb5 Black has an open a-file and queenside space, but the a8 rook stands on the bishop's diagonal with nothing guarding it, and one knight move from f3 uncovers the attack. Black has to spend time covering it; a sharp try that is easier to meet than to play.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop sits on the long diagonal where it presses on the centre and the queenside, and White can castle next. It fits the whole set-up, since Black's queenside fianchetto will meet it on the same diagonal.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bb7.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Queen's Indian Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bb7.strategy: The mirror move: the bishops face each other along the long diagonal with the f3 knight between them, and Black fights for e4 and d5 from a distance. A flexible, closed game follows in which neither side has yet fixed the centre.
